chapter_theme: In the last ilampakam Civakan preaches to his eight wives on giving, the foulness and fading of the body, and the fear of Death, and, when he tells them they are now strangers, they weep, fall at his feet and ask what fault they committed.

cast.role: the hero, now an old king, who preaches renunciation to his wives
Civakan's eight wives, who hear him and weep

2924.reading: As the conch and pearl are found only in the dark sea and never in a big pool, so the rare austerity that ripens from giving is found in few on earth, though lesser folk may share some of it.
2924.nuance: The last two lines turn on a doubtful syntax (மருங்குடை யவர்கட் கல்லான்); the contrast between the few and the rest is read from the sense, not fixed.

claims.claim: the rare austerity born of giving is found only in a few

2925.reading: As diamonds come only from the hill of the pouring stream and the blue lily blooms only in clear water, so only the noble share what they have; listen and ask, he says, for none else on earth does it.

claims.claim: only the noble share what they have with others

2926.reading: Though giving out of the offering-rice that women scatter in the temple is hard, one who gives the rare alms at every house-pillar of the women's homes gains a mountain of wealth.
2926.nuance: The picture of feeding at each pillar of a household is hard to place and the sense of 'offering' (பலி) is uncertain.

claims.claim: gifts of food given house after house turn into a mountain of wealth

2927.reading: Food given to the hungry that removes their distress and keeps their life is a well in the golden heaven, and one who guards every life and gives up honey and flesh has nothing to be said against him: earth and sky are his servants.

claims.claim: food given to the destitute is a well of reward in heaven
one who protects all lives and abstains from honey and flesh owns earth and sky

2928.reading: Kings who rule the world, after playing in the garden with bangled girls, are those who guard the habit of not drinking liquor, a small service.
2928.nuance: The verse names the cause only by hint (சிற்றுபகாரம், 'small help'); the later-birth reading is supplied from the sermon's frame.

claims.claim: a small kindness joined to abstaining from liquor brings kingship in a later birth

2929.reading: Those who never ate after giving stand shrinking in Masi-month cold, in cloth stitched from thorn-torn rags, begging 'a morsel' with the hand held out.
2929.nuance: The cause (never giving) is stated in the last line only; karma is implied, not named.
2929.event: Civakan shows his wives a beggar shivering in rags with an outstretched hand, who never gave.

claims.claim: beggary now is the fruit of never having given

2930.reading: Death is shown as a hunter driving a great deer in the forest, who, if we have no shelter, will mix up our lives and drink them like a ripened liquor he has laid by.
2930.nuance: Lines 1 and 2 are hard to parse (காட்டகத் தொருமகன் துரக்கும் மாக்கலை; ஓட்டுடைத் தாமெனின்) and the simile is read tentatively.

claims.claim: Death gathers and takes the life of all who have no refuge

2931.reading: Even from the hands of fowlers some birds escape; he bids the women look, and not dismiss with 'what' the word of a wise man, but learn the way of dharma.
2931.nuance: The addressee is the women; the bird image is read as an escape that dharma gives.

claims.claim: good deeds are a way of escape from Death, as some birds escape the fowler

2932.reading: The moon tells of dying, birth, growth and waning; to be angry with good dharma when it fails is what belongs to fools.
2932.nuance: Lines 3 and 4 are obscure (வாய்புகப் பெய்யினும் வழுக்கின்); the sense that scorn of dharma is folly is the best fit.

claims.claim: birth, growth, waning and death are the nature of all things, as the moon shows

2933.reading: A drop of water falls, grows within foul flesh and appears in a place; if the great virtue is thought of, the hut of flesh will be escaped and will yield only the pleasure of floods, so they say.
2933.nuance: Line 4's 'flood-water pleasure' is obscure; the verse is reported hearsay (என்பவே).

claims.claim: the body begins as a drop that grows in foul flesh
one who thinks of great dharma escapes the hut of flesh and gains lasting pleasure

2934.reading: Drops of milk and coral-water swell into flesh, it escapes by a narrow channel, then sinks in a pool of muddy water and, having no provision for the road, weeps and falls.
2934.nuance: 'Provision for the journey' (கால்துணா, line 4) is read as stored good deeds; the word is not explained in the verse.

claims.claim: birth is passage through foul water and a helpless fall, without provision of deeds for the next road

2935.reading: Good dharma is a golden wishing-tree that blossoms with wealth and pleasure, so though they are troubled, the women should not forget the way of dharma.

claims.claim: dharma yields wealth and enjoyment and must not be forgotten even in distress

2936.reading: Without charm and medicine no one would touch a five-headed snake; without the garland of bees, men would not come near women.
2936.nuance: The snake simile for desire is the sermon's; the verse's logic (adornments make desire) is inferred from the paired lines.

claims.claim: a woman's allure depends on her adornments, as a snake's danger is met only with charm and medicine

2937.reading: He tells the golden women that they shall give nothing but sweet liquid, and asks them to sit beside him and hear a few words, for they are worthy to win.
2937.nuance: Lines 1 and 2 are obscure (தருதும் பாகுநீர் தின்றலாற்); the speaker and the offer are read from the context.

2938.reading: Though the body smells strongly of sandal and flower, the sandal and flower are only what was put on by hand; underneath are fat, blood, oozing pus and soiled skin, and he asks if there is any lie in that.

claims.claim: the body is foul beneath its perfumes and ornaments

2939.reading: Like the anichcham flower they droop as soon as they are touched; we think 'we die from the day we are born', and what use is clear knowledge when, shaking and gazing about, one says 'we shall tremble'?
2939.nuance: The last two lines compress an argument; the sense that knowledge should be used before the shaking of death is read from the simile.

claims.claim: a person is dying from birth, so fear at the end shows knowledge has not been used

2940.reading: The blue colour of the five-part hair leaves, the breasts hang pale and sagging, the eyes lose their lustre and the body hides its colour: this, women, is not the body's true state.

claims.claim: youth's beauty fades and the body is not what it seems

2941.reading: The speaker, who ate rich food scented with ghee, fears the alms that must be begged in the great city, and says he will renounce but has no desire.
2941.nuance: Whether the fear of begging is the wives' answer to the sermon or part of Civakan's own argument is not settled; the verb துறப்பல் (I will renounce) and ஆர்வமில்லையே (there is no desire) may be read as a refusal.

claims.claim: renunciation requires giving up fine food and begging alms

2942.reading: Two who join in anger against one will break the strength of that one, he says to the slender-waisted, gem-adorned women.
2942.nuance: The argument is incomplete; the verse looks like an introduction to the renunciation announcement but the logic of two against one is not clear.

2943.reading: When the word that from the day love is gone they are strangers reached the women's ears, tears from their wide eyes poured down on their flowered breasts.
2943.event: The wives hear Civakan say that they are now strangers to him, and they weep.

2944.reading: The tears of the spear-eyed women, whose spear-like looks fed on flesh and killed kings, fall across the jewelled chains and gather in a pool, then pour down like a waterfall on their breasts.
2944.nuance: The simile of the waterfall is the narrator's; the opening 'ate flesh and killed kings' refers to the spear, not to the women.
2944.event: The wives weep until their tears flood their jewelled chests.

2945.reading: Like flowers fallen on the ground after a thunderbolt of harsh words, the garlanded women fall at the feet, fill a vessel with their tears and cry as their hair sways.
2945.event: The wives fall at Civakan's feet and weep.

2946.reading: They stand like a deer in the shadow of a tiger, their lives split, and ask what fault they committed under his feet, whose feet are like lotuses growing in red paste.
2946.event: The wives ask what wrong they did, and stand in terror.

2947.reading: The women say: see the thighs that bore us as a rare couch; do not think the women's lives will be pitiful and pained; look at the empty bodies when you stand like guests.
2947.nuance: The Tamil of lines 1-3 is dense; the sense of an appeal against the king's coldness is read from the whole.
2947.event: The wives appeal to Civakan to look at what is left of them as he stands like a guest.

2948.reading: Holding garland and cloth, applying kunkumam, putting pollen in their hair and stroking their breasts, those lovers' fingers are pitiable; you too became strangers and thought only of the king's mind.
2948.nuance: The speaker and the addressee are doubtful: the verse may be the wives' own reproach or the narrator's comment on them.

links.note: 2929 shows a man who never gave now begging in cold rags; 2624 shows a woman who drank boiled milk from a gold bowl now worn by hunger and cut off from her fortune.
links.teaches: The first pictures the beggar's state and names his past failure to give, the second pictures a fall from wealth, so together they show beggary as both the fruit of not giving and a turn of fortune.

links.note: 2929 says the beggar stands begging because he never gave; Naladiyar 107 says those who stand begging at great gates are living out their former deeds without saying which.
links.teaches: The epic names the former deed behind the begging, a life of not giving, where the quatrain leaves the cause as deeds in general.

gains.a: the beggar of the epic gains the Naladiyar's plain statement that begging in public is the working out of earlier deeds, not an accident
gains.b: the quatrain gains a named cause, never giving, for the former deeds that fill the begging bowl

links.note: 2927 makes food to the hungry a well in heaven and guarding life a title to earth and sky; Kural 222 says that even if there were no higher world, giving alone is good.
links.teaches: The epic gives the reward of heaven for giving, while the Kural says giving is right even with no reward, so the two differ on whether the gift needs a world to come.

gains.a: the heaven-reward of the verse is shown to be an extra, since the Kural holds giving good without it
gains.b: the Kural's no-heaven giving is given a school's account, Jain karma, in which giving does bring fruit

links.note: 2941's speaker, who ate rich ghee-scented food, fears the begging that renunciation brings; Naladiyar 1 says those who once ate six-flavoured food served by a willing wife may end up begging for gruel, so wealth is no support.
links.teaches: The quatrain uses the fall to beggary as the argument for renouncing, while the epic's speaker uses the same fall as the reason to fear renouncing.

gains.a: the speaker's fear of alms is answered, since the quatrain says such beggary comes anyway to the rich
gains.b: the quatrain's warning about lost wealth meets a person who feels it and still hesitates

links.note: 2938 strips the body of its sandal and flower to fat, blood, pus and soiled skin; Naladiyar 46 lists entrails, fat, blood, bone, sinew and skin and asks which part is the woman.
links.teaches: Both teach desire away by breaking the body into its parts, and the epic does it to the very women who are the audience.

gains.a: the verse's list of fluids gains the quatrain's question of where the woman is to be found among the parts
gains.b: the quatrain's analysis is placed in a scene where the one who is analysed is listening

links.note: 2934 follows the embryo through the channel and into muddy water where it falls weeping without provision for the road; Tirumanthiram 451 has the Lord stay within the womb and form the embryo.
links.teaches: One text lets the body come into the world helpless and left to its deeds, the other has a Lord who forms it, so the same birth is read without and with a maker.

gains.a: the epic's helpless birth meets a verse that says a Lord forms the embryo within the womb
gains.b: the Tirumanthiram's Lord within the womb is set against a Jain account of birth with no one forming it

links.note: 2940 shows the body's colour, breasts and eyes fading with age as the women watch; Siddhar 23 asks when the speaker will see the bones within as white bones and see himself lowered like a cast-off corpse.
links.teaches: The epic shows the body's fading from the lover's side, the Siddhar from the renouncer's, so one is a loss and the other is a practice.

gains.a: the verse's fading colour gains the Siddhar's practice of looking through the flesh to the bones
gains.b: the Siddhar's look at the bones gains a view of the same body as it loses its beauty to a lover

links.note: 2939 says we begin dying from the day we are born and knowledge is useless when one shakes at the end; 2616 has Vijayai say we are born not knowing our days and cover our eyes only when the cow is milked.
links.teaches: The mother's warning in the first sermon returns in the king's own words to his wives, so the doctrine is passed down rather than invented.

source_issues: Verses 2924-2927, 2938-2940 and 2944-2948 were printed in eight half-lines in the source and joined into four lines (FLAG repaired); the joins read correctly.
2924 lines 3-4, 2926, 2930 lines 1-2, 2932 lines 3-4, 2937 lines 1-2 and 2942 are hard to parse; readings are marked uncertain.
The speaker of 2941, 2942, 2947 and 2948 is not named in the Tamil and is inferred from context.
